ON THE 10th OF JULY, 2025  MISC. APPEAL No. 1338 of 2024  DECEASED SOHAN S/O AMARSINGH THROUGH LRS. PRAKASH  AND OTHERS  Versus  SANTOSH AND OTHERS  Appearance:
 Shri Himanshu Paliwal, learned counsel for the appell  Shri Manoj Jain, learned counsel for respondent No.3   Company.

ORDER The appellants have filed this Misc. Appeal under section 173(1) of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 being aggrieved by the award dated 04.10.2023 passed in Claim Case No.179/2021.
2.
Appellant No.1 is the brother of the deceased and appellants No.2 to 4 are the wife and children of appellant No.1.
3. The brief facts giving rise to this case are that on 02.02.2021, the deceased Sohan was sitting as a pillion rider on the motorbike of one Deepak.
They were going via Dhar Road to their Village Ajanda.
When they reached near Dadawadi, Dhar road, a Car bearing registration number MP- 11-CC-7857 came from the direction of Manawar.

The car driven by respondent No.1 / Santosh in a rash and negligent manner, collided with the motorbike, due to which Sohan sustained grievous injuries and died on the NEUTRAL CITATION NO. 2025:MPHC-IND:17587 2 MA-1338-2024 spot.

3.1. Regarding the accident, an FIR was registered at Crime No.132/2021 at Police Station Manawar,
dhar.
The appellants filed a claim petition under Section 166 of the Motor Vehicles Act seeking compensation for the death of Sohan.
The Claims Tribunal after considering the evidence on record concluded that the appellants were not dependents of the deceased.

Therefore, except under the head of dependency, compensation was awarded at Rs.44,000/- for loss of consortium to the brother of the deceased and Rs.16,500/- each for loss of estate and funeral expenses.
Thus, a total compensation of Rs.77,000/- was awarded.

sentences.text: Learned counsel for the appellant submits that it is undisputed that the deceased was the brother of appellant No.1.

Referring to the findings in paras 26 and 27 of the impugned award, he submits that the Claims Tribunal wrongly concluded that although the deceased was the brother of appellant No.1, the appellants were not dependent on the deceased.
He further submits that the appellants and the deceased were living in the same house and that the deceased contributed to the family income, therefore, the appellants are dependents of the deceased.

In support of his submission, he relies on the judgements of Hon'ble Apex Court in Sadhna Tomar and Ors. vs Ashok Kushwaha and Ors. reported in 2025 LiveLaw (SC) 309 and N. Jayashree and Others vs Cholamandalam MS General Insurance Company Limited in Civil Appeal No.6451/2021 and the judgment of the Calcutta High Court in Sk. Kader Ali and Orthers vs The Oriental Insurance Company Limited in FMA No.650/2007 with CAN 1 of 2008 (old No. CAN NEUTRAL CITATION NO.
2025:MPHC-IND:17587 3 MA-1338-2024 780 of 2008).

sentences.text: Per contra, learned counsel for the Insurance Company submits, with reference to the specific findings in para 27, that the deceased and appellant No.1 were four brothers, all are married and living separately, each having separate ration cards.
He specifically refers to the deposition of Prakash (AW-1), who admitted in his cross-examination that appellants No.2 to 4 are his wife and children and that they are dependent upon him.
He also refers to the findings in para 26, which record that the deceased was suffering from polio in both legs, a fact admitted by the appellant No.1 in his cross- examination.

6. He further submits that the Tribunal after considering that appellant No.1 is 40 years of age and a married man with his own family, held that he cannot be deemed or conceived to be dependent on a person suffering from polio in both legs.
Thus, he supports the findings of the award and prays for dismissal of the appeal.

In support of his submission, learned counsel for the Insurance Company relied on the case of National Insurance Company Ltd. vs Pranay Sethi reported in 2017 ACJ 2700 ,
particularly paras 31, 42(43.6) and 43.
7.

entities.text: National Insurance Company Ltd. vs Pranay Sethi reported in 2017 ACJ 2700
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: Heard learned counsel for the respective parties and perused the record.

8. There is no dispute regarding the preposition of law that even when the claimants are not the legal representatives in the broader sense under the law of succession, they can still be considered dependents of the deceased for NEUTRAL CITATION NO. 2025:MPHC-IND:17587 4 MA-1338-2024 the purposes of claims filed under the provisions of the Motor Vehicles Act.
9. Learned counsel for the appellants while relying on the above- mentioned decisions has tried to harp upon the fact that it is not necessary for a claimant to be a legal representatives of Class I.

His submission that even in cases, where there is no loss of dependency, a claimant who is a legal representatives would still be entitled to compensation is a misconception of the ratio of decidendi of the Hon'ble Apex Court in the aforementioned cases.

10. What now has been decided by the Hon'ble Apex Court is that the term "legal representatives"
should be given a wider interpretation for the purposes of Chapter XII of the Motor Vehicles Act and Deceased Sohan S/O Amarsingh Through ... vs Santosh on 10 July, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/15302594/
2 should not be confined only to mean the spouse, parents and children of the deceased.
In fact, this controversy has been conclusively put to rest by the Hon'ble Apex Court in the Larger Bench decision in National Insurance Company Ltd. vs Pranay Sethi reported in 2017 ACJ 2700 .

entities.text: National Insurance Company Ltd. vs Pranay Sethi reported in 2017 ACJ 2700
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text:
The Hon'ble Apex Court in paras 31, 42(43.6) and 43 of the same judgment has held as under :
"31.
Where the deceased was a bachelor and the claimants are the parents, the deduction follows a different principle.
In regard to bachelors, normally, 50% is deducted as personal and living expenses, because it is assumed that a bachelor would tend to spend more on himself.

Even otherwise, there is also the possibility of his getting married in a short time, in which event the contribution to the parent(s)
and siblings is likely to be cut drastically.

Further, subject to evidence to the contrary,
the father is likely to have his own income and will not be considered as a dependant and the mother alone will be considered as a dependant.
In the absence of evidence to the contrary, brothers and sisters will not be considered as dependants, because they will either be independent and earning, or married, or be dependent on the father.

43.6. Insofar as deduction for personal and living expenses is concerned, it is directed that the Tribunals shall ordinarily follow NEUTRAL CITATION NO.
2025:MPHC-IND:17587 5 MA-1338-2024 the standards prescribed in paras 30, 31 and 32 of the judgment in Sarla Verma subject to the observations made by us in para 41 above."

43. On a perusal of the analysis made in Sarla Verma which has been reconsidered in Reshma Kumari, we think it appropriate to state that as far as the guidance provided for appropriate deduction for personal and living expenses is concerned, the tribunals and courts should be guided by conclusion 43.6 of Reshma Kumari.
We concur with the same as we have no hesitation in approving the method provided therein."

11. It is thus clear that as per the ratio laid down in Pranay Sethi (Supra), in the absence of evidence to the contrary, brothers and sisters will not be considered dependents, as they are either independent and earning, married or dependent on their father.
12. In the present case, appellant No.1 has miserably failed to establish even a single fact relating to his dependency on the deceased.
He admitted in his cross-examination that the deceased was suffering from polio in both legs.
He also admitted that appellants No.2 to 4 are dependent on him i.e. appellant No.1.
No source of income of the deceased was brought on record.
13. Thus, keeping in view the facts on record in the present case, there appears to be no reason to interfere with the findings of the Claims Tribunal.
Resultantly, the instant appeal fails and is hereby dismissed.
No order as to costs.
